acceptedAnswer.text: Java Hashtable is a legacy synchronized Map implementation in the java.util package that stores key-value pairs in a hash table (bucket array). It has been part of Java since version 1.0, predating the Collections Framework. Every method in Hashtable is synchronized, making it thread-safe but slower than HashMap. It does not allow null keys or null values, unlike HashMap.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between Hashtable and HashMap in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Key differences: (1) Thread Safety — Hashtable is synchronized (thread-safe); HashMap is not. (2) Null Keys/Values — Hashtable allows neither null keys nor null values; HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values. (3) Performance — HashMap is faster in single-threaded scenarios because it has no synchronization overhead. (4) Legacy — Hashtable is a legacy class from Java 1.0; HashMap was added in Java 1.2 as part of the Collections Framework. (5) Iteration — Hashtable uses Enumeration (legacy); HashMap uses Iterator.

mainEntity.name: Is Hashtable still used in Java?

acceptedAnswer.text: Hashtable is considered a legacy class and is generally not recommended for new code. For non-thread-safe single-threaded use, prefer HashMap. For thread-safe multi-threaded use, prefer ConcurrentHashMap which offers much better concurrency through segment/bucket-level locking instead of Hashtable's coarse-grained whole-table locking. Hashtable exists mainly for backward compatibility with older codebases.

mainEntity.name: Can Hashtable have null keys or null values?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Hashtable does not allow null keys or null values. Attempting to put a null key or null value throws NullPointerException immediately. This is in contrast to HashMap which allows one null key and any number of null values. This restriction in Hashtable exists because its hashing mechanism calls key.hashCode() directly, which would throw NullPointerException on a null key.

mainEntity.name: What is the load factor in Hashtable?

acceptedAnswer.text: The load factor in Hashtable is a threshold that determines when the internal bucket array is resized (rehashed). The default load factor is 0.75 and the default initial capacity is 11. When the number of entries exceeds capacity × load factor, Hashtable rehashes — it creates a new bucket array of approximately 2× the old capacity and redistributes all existing entries. A lower load factor reduces collisions but wastes memory; a higher load factor saves memory but increases collisions and lookup time.

blocks.text: Java Hashtable is one of the oldest data structures in the Java standard library — it has existed since Java 1.0, predating the entire Collections Framework. It implements the Map<K, V> interface and stores data as key-value pairs inside an internal array of buckets, using a hash function to determine where each entry is placed.

The defining characteristic of Hashtable is that every public method is synchronized, making it inherently thread-safe. This was the primary reason for its existence in Java's early days when thread-safe maps were a necessity and no better alternative existed. However, this coarse-grained locking strategy — locking the entire table for every operation — makes it significantly slower than modern alternatives in multi-threaded environments.

Hashtable has two firm rules that distinguish it from HashMap: it does not allow null keys and it does not allow null values. Attempting to insert either immediately throws a NullPointerException. It also does not maintain insertion order, and iteration order is not guaranteed to be consistent across JVM versions.

Today, Hashtable is considered a legacy class. The Java documentation itself recommends using HashMap for non-concurrent scenarios and ConcurrentHashMap for thread-safe scenarios. Understanding Hashtable remains important for maintaining legacy codebases and for Java interviews, where its differences from HashMap are among the most commonly tested topics.

sections.title: Internal Structure — How Hashtable Works Under the Hood

blocks.text: Hashtable internally uses an array of Entry (bucket) objects. Each bucket is the head of a singly linked list (chain) of entries that share the same hash bucket — this technique for resolving collisions is called separate chaining.

Entry<K,V>  next;   // next entry in the same bucket (chaining)
private transient Entry<?,?>[] table;   // the bucket array
private transient int count;             // total number of entries
private int threshold;                   // count at which rehash occurs (capacity × loadFactor)
// threshold = 11 × 0.75 = 8  →  rehash when 9th entry is added

blocks.text: Key difference from HashMap internals: HashMap uses the initial capacity of 16 (power of two) and computes the bucket index using bitwise AND: index = hash & (capacity - 1). Hashtable uses the initial capacity of 11 (prime number) and computes bucket index using modulo: index = (hash & 0x7FFFFFFF) % capacity. The prime-number capacity in Hashtable was historically chosen to reduce clustering, though modern implementations have moved to power-of-two sizing with better hash spreading.
Hashtable sits in a unique position in the Java type hierarchy — it extends Dictionary, a legacy abstract class from Java 1.0, while also implementing the modern Map interface added in Java 1.2.

sections.title: Load Factor and Rehashing in Hashtable

blocks.text: Two of the most important performance-tuning concepts in Hashtable are load factor and rehashing. Understanding them helps you configure Hashtable (and its modern successor HashMap) for optimal performance.

items.text: — A float value between 0.0 and 1.0 that controls the fill-threshold of the bucket array. Default is 0.75f. When the number of entries exceeds capacity × loadFactor, the table is rehashed. Formula: threshold = capacity × loadFactor. With default values: threshold = 11 × 0.75 = 8. The 9th insertion triggers rehashing.

— When the threshold is exceeded, Hashtable creates a new bucket array with capacity approximately 2× the old capacity + 1 (e.g., 11 → 23 → 47 → ...). Every existing entry is re-inserted into the new array using the new modulo calculation. Rehashing is O(n) and synchronized — a full table lock is held for the entire duration, which is a major concurrency bottleneck.
— Fewer collisions, faster lookups — but higher memory usage because the table is kept mostly empty. Rehashing occurs more frequently.
— Memory-efficient — table stays dense — but more collisions occur. Lookup degrades as chains grow longer. Rehashing occurs rarely.

— The default load factor of 0.75 is carefully chosen to balance memory and performance. Only deviate if you have profiling data showing it is a bottleneck. If final table size is known in advance, set initialCapacity = expectedSize / loadFactor + 1 to avoid any rehashing at all.

blocks.text: Decision Rule: In 2026, there is almost never a reason to use Hashtable in new code. Use HashMap for single-threaded code. Use ConcurrentHashMap for multi-threaded code. The only valid reason to keep Hashtable in a codebase is legacy compatibility or when the existing API contract requires it (e.g., when a Properties subclass is required).

sections.title: Thread Safety in Hashtable — How It Works and Why It Falls Short

blocks.text: Hashtable achieves thread safety by declaring every public method with the synchronized keyword. This means only one thread can execute any Hashtable operation at a time — even two threads doing concurrent reads must wait for each other.

blocks.text: Critical insight: Hashtable's method-level synchronization guarantees that no two threads execute the same method simultaneously, but it does not guarantee atomicity of compound operations like check-then-act or read-modify-write patterns. For true thread-safe atomic operations, use ConcurrentHashMap's compute(), merge(), or computeIfAbsent().

blocks.text: Most best practices for Hashtable center around one theme: knowing when NOT to use it and what to use instead. When you do encounter it in a codebase, follow these guidelines.

items.text: — If you need a synchronized map in new code, always use ConcurrentHashMap. It offers far better concurrency through bucket-level (fine-grained) locking — multiple threads can read and write to different buckets simultaneously, unlike Hashtable which serializes every operation.
— If thread safety is not needed, HashMap is always faster. It has zero synchronization overhead and allows null keys and values.
— Declare variables as Map<K,V> rather than Hashtable<K,V>. This allows switching to HashMap or ConcurrentHashMap with a one-line change when requirements change.

— If you know the approximate number of entries, set initialCapacity = expectedSize / 0.75 + 1. Rehashing is O(n) and acquires a full table lock — it is both CPU-expensive and a concurrency bottleneck.

items.strong: ✅ 5. Always Override hashCode() and equals() for Custom Keys
items.text: — If you use a custom class as a Hashtable key, both methods must be correctly overridden and consistent with each other. A broken hashCode() scatters equal keys across different buckets, making lookups return null even when the key exists.
— Avoid the legacy keys() and elements() Enumeration methods. Use forEach(BiConsumer), entrySet() iteration, or stream() for cleaner, more readable code.

items.strong: ❌ 7. Do Not Use Hashtable for Compound Operations
items.text: — get() followed by put() is NOT atomic even in Hashtable. Between the two synchronized calls, another thread can modify the value. Use ConcurrentHashMap.compute(), computeIfAbsent(), or merge() for truly atomic compound operations.
— Extending Hashtable to add behavior is an anti-pattern. The only legitimate subclass in the JDK is Properties. Prefer composition over inheritance for adding functionality to a map.

blocks.text: Practice This Code — Live Editor
Hashtable is a battle-tested but outdated data structure. Its advantages were once compelling; today they are largely superseded by better alternatives.

pros.title: Built-in Thread Safety
pros.text: Every public method is synchronized — no external synchronization required for basic operations. In Java's early days (pre-1.2), this was the only way to get a thread-safe map without writing your own.

pros.title: No Null Key/Value — Fail Fast
pros.text: Rejecting null keys and values immediately with NullPointerException prevents silent null-related bugs that can be hard to diagnose in HashMap-based code.

pros.title: Properties Subclass Ecosystem
pros.text: java.util.Properties extends Hashtable and is the foundation for Java's configuration file system. Working with .properties files, System properties, or Maven/Gradle configurations all involve Hashtable indirectly.

pros.title: Long-Standing Stability
pros.text: Hashtable has been in Java since version 1.0. Its behavior is exhaustively documented and well-understood. In legacy systems, its predictable (if slow) behavior is sometimes preferred over introducing newer dependencies.

pros.title: Works with Legacy APIs
pros.text: Some older Java APIs and frameworks explicitly expect Hashtable or its subclasses. In those contexts, Hashtable remains the only correct choice without refactoring the API contract.

cons.title: Coarse-Grained Locking Kills Concurrency
cons.text: The whole-table lock means only one thread executes any operation at a time. Under high concurrency, threads queue up waiting for the lock — causing severe throughput degradation compared to ConcurrentHashMap.

cons.title: Poor Performance Even in Single-Threaded Code
cons.text: Even with no concurrent threads, every Hashtable call acquires and releases a monitor lock. This synchronization overhead makes it measurably slower than HashMap for single-threaded workloads.

cons.title: Legacy API — Not Recommended for New Code
cons.text: Java documentation explicitly marks Hashtable as a legacy class. Its design predates the Collections Framework, and it carries baggage like the Dictionary superclass and Enumeration iteration that have no place in modern Java.

cons.title: No Null Support Creates Rigid Constraints
cons.text: While null rejection can prevent some bugs, it also means you cannot use null as a sentinel value for 'not found' or 'uninitialized'. Code that naturally uses null keys or values must be redesigned to use Hashtable.

cons.title: Compound Operations Are Not Atomic
cons.text: Individual method calls are synchronized but compound operations (containsKey then put, get then put) are not. This creates a false sense of safety — developers assume Hashtable is fully thread-safe and miss race conditions in compound logic.

cons.title: Unordered and Unpredictable Iteration Order
cons.text: Like HashMap, Hashtable provides no ordering guarantees. Unlike LinkedHashMap (insertion order) or TreeMap (sorted order), there is no way to get predictable iteration order from a Hashtable.

blocks.text: These are the most frequently asked interview questions on Java Hashtable for Java developer positions. The Hashtable vs HashMap comparison is especially common in technical interviews.

items.q: Q1. What is Hashtable in Java? How is it different from HashMap?
items.a: Hashtable is a legacy synchronized Map implementation from Java 1.0 using a bucket array with chaining for collision resolution. Key differences: (1) Hashtable is synchronized (thread-safe); HashMap is not. (2) Hashtable does not allow null keys or values; HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values. (3) HashMap is faster in single-threaded code due to no lock overhead. (4) Hashtable uses a prime initial capacity (11); HashMap uses a power-of-two (16).

items.q: Q2. Why is Hashtable considered a legacy class in Java?
items.a: Hashtable predates the Collections Framework (Java 1.2). It extends the obsolete Dictionary abstract class rather than AbstractMap. Its coarse-grained whole-table locking is inferior to ConcurrentHashMap's fine-grained locking. Its Enumeration-based iteration is superseded by Iterator. The Java documentation itself recommends HashMap or ConcurrentHashMap for all new code. Hashtable exists solely for backward compatibility.

items.q: Q3. What happens if you put a null key or null value into a Hashtable?
items.a: Both throw NullPointerException immediately — not when the key is later looked up, but at the moment of the put() call. This is because Hashtable calls key.hashCode() directly without a null check. In contrast, HashMap handles null keys specially by assigning them to bucket 0 and using == null comparisons instead of equals(). This is one of the most frequently tested Hashtable differences.

items.q: Q4. Is Hashtable fully thread-safe? Can race conditions still occur?
items.a: Hashtable is thread-safe at the individual method level — each method call is atomically synchronized. However, compound operations (check-then-act, read-modify-write) are NOT atomic. For example: if (!ht.containsKey(k)) { ht.put(k, v); } — between containsKey() and put(), another thread can insert the same key. For atomic compound operations, use ConcurrentHashMap's compute(), putIfAbsent(), or merge().

items.q: Q5. What is the default initial capacity and load factor of Hashtable?
items.a: Default initial capacity is 11 (a prime number — historically chosen to reduce hash clustering with the modulo-based bucket index). Default load factor is 0.75. The initial threshold is 11 × 0.75 = 8, meaning rehashing is triggered when the 9th entry is inserted. Compare to HashMap which defaults to capacity 16 (power of two) with the same 0.75 load factor.

items.q: Q6. What is the difference between Hashtable and ConcurrentHashMap?
items.a: Both are thread-safe, but their locking strategies differ fundamentally. Hashtable uses coarse-grained locking — the entire table is locked for every operation, serializing all threads. ConcurrentHashMap uses fine-grained (bucket/segment-level) locking — multiple threads can concurrently read and write to different buckets. ConcurrentHashMap also supports atomic compound operations (compute, merge, computeIfAbsent). ConcurrentHashMap is the modern replacement for Hashtable in concurrent code.

items.q: Q7. What is the difference between keys() and keySet() in Hashtable?
items.a: keys() returns a legacy Enumeration<K> — an older Java 1.0 iteration interface that only supports hasMoreElements() and nextElement(). keySet() returns a Set<K> backed by the Hashtable — a modern Collection that supports Iterator, for-each, stream(), and remove-during-iteration via iterator.remove(). Always prefer keySet() (or entrySet() / forEach) over keys() in new or refactored code.

items.q: Q8. Does Hashtable maintain insertion order?
items.a: No. Hashtable does not guarantee any iteration order. The order depends on the hash codes of keys and the bucket layout — it can appear random and may change after rehashing. If you need predictable order: use LinkedHashMap for insertion-order, TreeMap for sorted order, or iterate and sort separately. This is the same limitation as HashMap.

items.q: Q9. What class extends Hashtable in the Java standard library?
items.a: java.util.Properties extends Hashtable<Object, Object>. Properties is used throughout Java for configuration files (.properties), system properties (System.getProperties()), and application settings. When you call System.getProperty("java.version") or load a .properties file with Properties.load(InputStream), you are working with a Hashtable subclass.

items.q: Q10. How does rehashing work in Hashtable, and why is it a concurrency concern?
items.a: Rehashing is triggered when count exceeds threshold (capacity × loadFactor). Hashtable creates a new bucket array with capacity ≈ 2 × old + 1, then re-inserts all existing entries by recomputing bucket indices for the new capacity. The entire rehash operation is performed under the Hashtable's synchronized lock — blocking ALL other threads from any read or write for the full duration of the rehash. For large tables, this can cause significant latency spikes. ConcurrentHashMap avoids this by rehashing per-segment, minimizing blocking.

blocks.text: Test your understanding of Hashtable with these practice questions. Try answering each one before revealing the answer.

items.a: Output: 2 3. Hashtable does not allow duplicate keys. The second put("A", 3) overwrites the first value 1 with 3. The table still has only 2 entries ("A" and "B"), so size() returns 2. get("A") returns the latest value 3.

items.q: 2. Which of the following will throw NullPointerException in Hashtable? (a) ht.get(null) (b) ht.put("key", null) (c) ht.put(null, "value") (d) ht.containsValue(null)
items.a: (a) get(null) — NullPointerException (null key not allowed). (b) put("key", null) — NullPointerException (null value not allowed). (c) put(null, "value") — NullPointerException (null key not allowed). (d) containsValue(null) — this ALSO throws NullPointerException in Hashtable. All four throw NPE. In HashMap, all four would work without exception.

items.q: 3. Two threads, T1 and T2, both execute: if (!ht.containsKey("seat")) { ht.put("seat", threadName); } on the same Hashtable. Can both threads add an entry for "seat"?
items.a: Yes — this is a classic check-then-act race condition. Although containsKey() and put() are individually synchronized, they are not synchronized together as a unit. T1 calls containsKey() → false (seat is empty). Before T1 calls put(), T2 also calls containsKey() → false. Both then call put(). The second put() overwrites the first. The correct fix is ConcurrentHashMap.putIfAbsent("seat", threadName) which is atomic.

items.q: 4. You are maintaining legacy code that uses Hashtable. A new requirement needs null values to represent 'not yet assigned'. What is your approach?
items.a: Hashtable cannot store null values — NullPointerException will be thrown. Options: (1) Replace Hashtable with HashMap (preferred if thread safety is not needed, or use ConcurrentHashMap if it is). (2) Use a sentinel object (e.g., a static final UNASSIGNED = new Object()) as a placeholder instead of null. (3) Use Optional<V> as the value type — but this adds complexity. The cleanest solution is migration to HashMap or ConcurrentHashMap.

items.q: 5. A Hashtable has initialCapacity=11, loadFactor=0.75. After how many put() calls will the first rehash occur?
items.a: threshold = floor(11 × 0.75) = floor(8.25) = 8. Rehashing is triggered when count exceeds threshold — i.e., when the 9th entry is inserted. So after exactly 9 put() calls (assuming all distinct keys), the first rehash occurs. The new capacity becomes approximately 2 × 11 + 1 = 23.

Output: 10 10. putIfAbsent("X", "99") checks if "X" is already present. It is — with value "10". So the value is NOT changed. putIfAbsent() returns the existing value ("10") and leaves the table unchanged. ht.get("X") still returns "10".

items.q: 7. Why does Hashtable use a prime number (11) as its default initial capacity while HashMap uses a power of two (16)?
items.a: Hashtable uses modulo for bucket index: (hash & 0x7FFFFFFF) % capacity. Prime capacities tend to distribute keys more uniformly with this method because prime moduli reduce clustering patterns in hash distributions. HashMap uses bitwise AND for bucket index: hash & (capacity - 1), which only works correctly (and efficiently) with power-of-two capacities. HashMap compensates for power-of-two clustering by applying a supplemental hash spreading function (key.hashCode() XOR with its own right-shifted bits).

items.q: 8. In terms of memory, what does each entry in a Hashtable cost compared to a plain key-value pair?
items.a: Each entry in Hashtable is wrapped in an Entry object containing: (1) int hash — 4 bytes cached hash, (2) K key reference — 4 or 8 bytes, (3) V value reference — 4 or 8 bytes, (4) Entry next reference — 4 or 8 bytes (for chaining), plus JVM object header — typically 12–16 bytes. On a 64-bit JVM with compressed oops, each Entry object is approximately 32 bytes in addition to the actual key and value objects. This overhead compounds with large tables and makes Hashtable more memory-intensive than a simple flat array map.

sections.title: Conclusion — Understanding Hashtable's Place in Java

blocks.text: Hashtable occupies a unique place in Java history — it was Java's first key-value data structure, it powered the early years of Java enterprise development, and it introduced the concept of synchronized collections to the JVM ecosystem. Understanding it deeply means understanding why better alternatives like HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap were designed the way they were.

In modern Java development, Hashtable is a museum piece — worth understanding thoroughly for interviews and legacy maintenance, but almost never the right choice for new code. Its coarse-grained locking, null restrictions, and legacy API make it strictly inferior to its successors in every scenario.

rows: ✅ Use HashMap — faster, allows null, modern API
✅ Use ConcurrentHashMap — fine-grained locking, atomic compound ops
✅ Use Properties (Hashtable subclass — this is correct and necessary)
⚠️ Keep as-is unless refactoring; document the legacy context
Tempted to use Hashtable for thread safety
❌ Use ConcurrentHashMap instead — strictly better in every way

blocks.text: Your next steps: study HashMap internals (Java 8's treeification of long chains), ConcurrentHashMap's segment architecture, and the Map interface contract in depth. Together, these form the backbone of key-value storage in virtually every Java application ever written. ☕

items.q: What is Hashtable in Java?
items.a: Java Hashtable is a legacy synchronized Map implementation in the java.util package that stores key-value pairs in a hash table (bucket array). It has been part of Java since version 1.0, predating the Collections Framework. Every method in Hashtable is synchronized, making it thread-safe but slower than HashMap. It does not allow null keys or null values, unlike HashMap.

items.q: What is the difference between Hashtable and HashMap in Java?
items.a: Key differences: (1) Thread Safety — Hashtable is synchronized (thread-safe); HashMap is not. (2) Null Keys/Values — Hashtable allows neither null keys nor null values; HashMap allows one null key and multiple null values. (3) Performance — HashMap is faster in single-threaded scenarios because it has no synchronization overhead. (4) Legacy — Hashtable is a legacy class from Java 1.0; HashMap was added in Java 1.2 as part of the Collections Framework. (5) Iteration — Hashtable uses Enumeration (legacy); HashMap uses Iterator.

items.q: Is Hashtable still used in Java?
items.a: Hashtable is considered a legacy class and is generally not recommended for new code. For non-thread-safe single-threaded use, prefer HashMap. For thread-safe multi-threaded use, prefer ConcurrentHashMap which offers much better concurrency through segment/bucket-level locking instead of Hashtable's coarse-grained whole-table locking. Hashtable exists mainly for backward compatibility with older codebases.

items.q: Can Hashtable have null keys or null values?
items.a: No. Hashtable does not allow null keys or null values. Attempting to put a null key or null value throws NullPointerException immediately. This is in contrast to HashMap which allows one null key and any number of null values. This restriction in Hashtable exists because its hashing mechanism calls key.hashCode() directly, which would throw NullPointerException on a null key.

items.q: What is the load factor in Hashtable?
items.a: The load factor in Hashtable is a threshold that determines when the internal bucket array is resized (rehashed). The default load factor is 0.75 and the default initial capacity is 11. When the number of entries exceeds capacity × load factor, Hashtable rehashes — it creates a new bucket array of approximately 2× the old capacity and redistributes all existing entries. A lower load factor reduces collisions but wastes memory; a higher load factor saves memory but increases collisions and lookup time.
